prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT diagnose viral (aseptic) meningitis and withhold IV antibiotics solely because Gram stain and culture are negative, when the patient has received prior oral antibiotics and CSF biochemistry shows low glucose, high protein, and elevated lactate.
Do NOT stop or downgrade empiric IV antibiotic therapy because blood cultures are negative; antibiotic pretreatment explains culture sterilization.
Do NOT delay empiric IV antibiotic therapy while awaiting multiplex PCR results when clinical and CSF features are consistent with bacterial meningitis.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do NOT treat with continuation of oral amoxicillin alone; CNS penetration of oral amoxicillin at standard sinusitis doses is inadequate for bacterial meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: S. pneumoniae is identified.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 14, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Recognize that a negative Gram stain and a culture without growth after 3.5 days of oral amoxicillin do not exclude bacterial meningitis: partial treatment explains them.
Use the CSF multiplex PCR, which stays positive after antibiotic pretreatment, to identify the organism when Gram stain and culture are negative.
Use the CSF biochemistry (lactate above 3.5 mmol/L, CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less, neutrophil predominance) to separate partially treated bacterial meningitis from viral meningitis.
Draw two sets of blood cultures before the first IV antibiotic dose, even though they are likely to be negative after amoxicillin.
With S. pneumoniae identified by PCR and no isolate for susceptibility testing, continue ceftriaxone as the definitive agent.
Stop ibuprofen while on dexamethasone (gastrointestinal bleeding risk).
Ask ENT to assess the right maxillary and ethmoid sinus disease as the likely parameningeal source.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

differential.key_features: The trap: negative Gram stain and no growth after amoxicillin, with a lymphocytic share in the CSF. Excluded: neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis (54%), CSF:blood glucose ratio 0.37, lactate 4.6 mmol/L and S. pneumoniae on multiplex PCR, with no viral target detected.
Mixed pleocytosis, low glucose and high protein also occur in TB meningitis; excluded by the 36-hour onset after a sinus infection, neutrophil predominance and S. pneumoniae on PCR.
HSV can present with fever, headache and confusion; excluded by negative HSV-1/2 PCR on the multiplex panel and absence of focal deficits.
Excluded in this immunocompetent, HIV-negative patient by negative cryptococcal antigen and India ink.

Ibuprofen use noted; ibuprofen-induced aseptic meningitis gives a neutrophilic pleocytosis but a normal glucose ratio and no organism, unlike the ratio of 0.37, lactate of 4.6 mmol/L and S. pneumoniae on PCR here.

key_clinical_evidence: Prior oral antibiotic therapy (amoxicillin 3.5 days) sterilizes CSF cultures in up to 30% of cases and reduces Gram stain sensitivity to as low as 40-60%; a negative Gram stain and culture must be interpreted in the context of antibiotic pretreatment, not used to rule out bacterial meningitis.

Multiplex PCR meningitis panels (e.g., BioFire FilmArray) detect bacterial DNA that persists even after antibiotic-induced culture sterilization; sensitivity for S. pneumoniae is maintained for at least 48-72 hours after antibiotic initiation.

CSF lactate >3.5-4 mmol/L is a strong discriminator for bacterial over viral meningitis, even in partially-treated cases, because it reflects host metabolic response to bacterial infection rather than viable organism burden.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

The mixed pleocytosis (PMN:lymphocyte ratio shifted toward lymphocytes) is characteristic of partial antibiotic treatment; it reflects partial PMN kill and does not indicate a primary lymphocytic (viral) process.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 14, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilledema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior beta-lactam therapy sterilizes CSF cultures and reduces Gram stain sensitivity; a negative Gram stain and a culture without growth in a partially treated patient do not exclude bacterial meningitis. Multiplex PCR identifies the organism, and the CSF biochemistry (low glucose ratio, high lactate) supports a bacterial cause.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative CSF Gram stain, and CSF culture with no growth at 48 hours, after 3.5 days of amoxicillin
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor the diagnostic reasoning toward viral or aseptic meningitis; an agent may prematurely conclude 'culture-negative meningitis = viral' and withhold IV antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Oral amoxicillin at sinusitis doses achieves inadequate CNS drug levels for bacterial meningitis; the prior antibiotic course explains the negative culture and Gram stain while the infection progressed, and is not evidence of adequate treatment.
red_herrings.data_point: Amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily prescribed 4 days before presentation for sinusitis, listed in current medications
red_herrings.intended_effect: The antibiotic history may be overlooked or interpreted as 'already treating the infection adequately' rather than recognized as the cause of the partially-treated CSF pattern.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Partial antibiotic pretreatment shifts the CSF differential from a pure PMN predominance toward a mixed pattern; this is a recognized hallmark of partially-treated bacterial meningitis and should not be interpreted as primary evidence for viral meningitis.
red_herrings.data_point: Mixed (not purely neutrophilic) CSF pleocytosis: 54% PMN, 39% lymphocytes
red_herrings.intended_effect: The lymphocytic component of the pleocytosis may suggest a viral or subacute infectious etiology rather than acute bacterial meningitis.

metadata.clinical_notes: This case tests whether the agent recognizes the partially-treated meningitis pattern: Gram stain and culture sterilized by prior oral amoxicillin, while multiplex PCR identifies S. pneumoniae and CSF biochemistry (lactate 4.6 mmol/L, glucose ratio 0.37) supports a bacterial etiology.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required tools; 3 embedded red herrings (negative Gram stain and culture, prior antibiotic course, mixed pleocytosis); tests resistance to the 'negative culture = not bacterial' anchor, the classic partially-treated meningitis diagnostic puzzle
metadata.revision_reason: Reviewer 2 meningitis audit: complete LP/microbiology/lab pathway, no ECG, and MRI restricted to complications or non-response
teaching_points: Prior antibiotic therapy sterilizes CSF cultures and reduces Gram stain sensitivity — always ask about recent antibiotic use when evaluating for meningitis
Multiplex PCR is indispensable in partially-treated meningitis and must be specifically ordered when Gram stain and culture are negative in a clinically suspicious case
CSF lactate and glucose ratio remain reliable discriminators in partially-treated bacterial meningitis even when culture-based tests are negative
The partially-treated CSF pattern — mixed rather than purely neutrophilic pleocytosis — should raise, not lower, suspicion for bacterial etiology when antibiotic pretreatment is known

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 33-year-old right-handed software engineer of South Asian descent who presents to the emergency department with a 24-hour history of severely worsening headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and fever, despite being on oral antibiotics. Approximately one week prior to presentation, he developed nasal congestion, mild sore throat, and low-grade fever that he attributed to a respiratory illness circulating among his colleagues following a large work conference. Four days before presentation, he visited an urgent care clinic where he was evaluated for worsening facial pressure and purulent nasal discharge. The clinician diagnosed presumed sinusitis and prescribed amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily. He began the antibiotic that evening and completed approximately 3.5 days of the course. His nasal symptoms initially improved modestly over the first two days of antibiotic therapy. However, approximately 36 hours before presentation, he developed a new, diffuse, severe bifrontal headache rated 9 out of 10 in intensity, which he describes as unlike any headache he has had before — constant, pressure-like, and worsened by movement, coughing, and bending forward. He noticed his neck becoming stiff over the same period, initially attributing it to muscle tension, and over the past 24 hours he has developed marked photophobia and phonophobia. His wife measured his temperature at 38.3 degrees Celsius this morning. He vomited once on arrival to the ED. He continued taking ibuprofen and amoxicillin up until this morning without significant relief. He denies any rash, seizures, focal limb weakness, vision changes, ear pain, or dental problems. He has no history of prior meningitis, neurosurgical procedures, or lumbar punctures. His wife brought him to the ED after he seemed to struggle recalling a colleague's phone number — a task he normally does effortlessly. He had no known direct contact with anyone diagnosed with meningitis.

Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline, no fasciculations.
